description:
List every block type this build can place in a model, with a one-line
summary and its required parameters.

Use this FIRST when you are about to build a model and do not yet know the
vocabulary. The `type` strings it returns are exactly what `add_block`
expects. Plugin block types appear here automatically.

Returns {"block_types": [{"type", "summary", "required", "multi_output"}]}.
`multi_output` marks the only types allowed more than one outgoing link
(DECIDE, LOGIC): every other block may have at most one.
name: list_block_types

description:
Describe one block type: what it does and every parameter with its type,
default and meaning.

Use this before `add_block`/`update_block` whenever you are unsure which
params a type takes -- passing an unknown key is an error, and the defaults
tell you what you may safely leave out. Each description is its first
sentence unless `detail` is true.

Returns {"type", "description", "multi_output", "params": [{"name", "type",
"default", "required", "description"}]}.

detail.description: Every description in full; by default each is its first sentence.

name: describe_block_type

description:
List the distribution names available for a duration or a random draw.

Pass `block_type` (CREATE, DELAY, PROCESS, ...) to get only the ones that
block is usually given; omit it for everything, including plugin entries.
The names are what goes in a block's `distribution` param, a link delay, or
a failure's uptime/downtime.

Returns {"distributions": [{"name", "category", "arrival", "delay",
"params"}]}; call describe_distribution for parameter meanings.

block_type.description: Optional block type (e.g. "CREATE", "DELAY") to list only the distributions offered for it; omit for the whole catalogue.

name: list_distributions

description:
Describe one distribution: when to use it and what each parameter means.

Use it when choosing between, say, Exponential and Lognormal for a service
time, or when you need the exact parameter names for `dist_params`. Every
numeric parameter also accepts an expression string, so a rate may depend
on an entity attribute.

Returns {"name", "category", "use_case", "support_lower", "params":
[{"name", "default", "hint", "kind"}]}.
name: describe_distribution

description:
Explain the expression language used by ASSIGN, DECIDE/HOLD conditions,
RECORD, ranking expressions and expression-valued distribution parameters.

Read this before writing any expression: it is a restricted-Python subset
(an AST allow-list, never eval), so anything not listed here is refused at
validation time rather than at run time.

Returns {"names", "operators", "functions": [{"name", "arity", "note"}],
"reserved", "examples"}.
name: get_expression_help

description:
Create an empty model in the workspace under *name*.

This is the starting point for building a model from a description: create
it, add blocks, connect them, then validate. Nothing is written to disk
until you call `save_model`. An empty model validates and runs, and
answers nothing: the first problems appear with the first block.

Returns the usual edit answer: {"ok", "introduced", "fixed", "errors",
"warnings", "model"}.

name.description: Workspace name for the new model (your handle for it later).

name: new_model

description:
Load a model file from the workspace root into the workspace.

Use it to inspect, modify or run an existing model, including the bundled
examples once they have been copied into the root. Older schema versions
migrate on load, so what you get back is always the current format.

Returns {"ok", "model", "path", "blocks", "errors", "warnings", "problems"}.

name.description: Workspace name to load it under; defaults to the file stem.

path.description: Model .json path, relative to the workspace root.

name: open_model

description:
Translate an XMILE (Stella/iThink) system-dynamics file into a new model.

Reads stocks, flows, auxiliaries, graphical functions (as lookup tables)
and dimensions (as subscripts) with a small expression translator, into
the workspace under *name*, exactly like `open_model` does for a model
JSON file. The file must be under the workspace root -- a path that
escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.

A construct this cannot translate (a module, a macro, a conveyor/queue
stock, a dimension mapping, an unknown function or name) is reported in
`import_problems` (code `E_SDIMPORT_UNSUPPORTED`) and left out of the model rather than guessed at; an approximation (a bare
DELAY, a non-euler/rk4 method, ...) is `W_SDIMPORT_APPROX`. Vensim `.mdl`
is not supported.

Returns {"ok", "model", "path", "import_problems": [{"code", "severity",
"message", "path", "hint"}], "errors", "warnings", "problems"} -- the last
three are the usual model-validation answer, over what DID translate.

name.description: Workspace name to load it under; defaults to the file stem.

path.description: XMILE (.xmile/.stmx) file, relative to the workspace root.

name: import_xmile

description:
Draft a model from an event log: what happened to each case, activity by activity.

The log needs a case id, an activity and a timestamp per row (CSV), or XES traces;
lifecycle (schedule/start/complete) and resource columns make the draft better. The
draft has one CREATE fitted to the case arrivals, one block per activity with its fitted
time, routing from the observed transitions and resources from the resource column,
and opens in the workspace under *name* like `open_model`. Nothing is written to disk.

It is a first draft: read `assumptions` (what the log could not tell, such as shifts or
the wait before a case's first activity) and `dropped` before trusting its numbers.
The file must be under the workspace root; a log over a size ceiling, or an XES file
with a DOCTYPE, is refused outright, and there is no argument that changes either.

Returns {"ok", "model", "routing", "activities": [{"block", "original", "count",
"lifecycle", "distribution", "mean", "mean_wait", "resource"}], "resources",
"activities_total", "resources_total", "assumptions", "dropped", "check": {"verdict",
"findings": [{"level", "what", "means"}]} (is the log good enough, and what each gap
means for the draft), "next_steps": {"check", "never"} (what to check in the draft, and
what this log cannot tell), "observed", "errors", "warnings", "problems"}, and with
*idle_waits* "idle_waits": [{"block", "delay"}] (the activities that got a modelled wait).
The two lists are cut to fit one reply; the totals say how many there are, and the open
model has them all.

idle_waits.description: true: each activity that waits long at mostly idle resources gets a DELAY before it, fitted to its waits (a modelled wait, not a queue); false (default): no such delay.

name.description: Workspace name to open the draft under; defaults to the file stem.

path.description: Event log (CSV, or .xes), relative to the workspace root.

routing.description: "auto" (a test on the log picks), "markov" (chances to the next activity) or "variants" (one routing per observed sequence).

time_unit.description: The draft's time unit: seconds, minutes, hours or days. A numeric timestamp is taken as already in it.

name: import_event_log

description:
Translate a Vensim system-dynamics file into a new model.

Reads equations, INTEG stocks, an inline `WITH LOOKUP` (as a lookup table) and
subscript ranges with a small stdlib reader (no `pysd`), into the workspace under
*name*, exactly like `open_model` does for a model JSON file. The file must be
under the workspace root -- a path that escapes it is refused, and there is no
argument that widens that.

A construct this cannot translate (a `:MACRO:`, `GET XLS/DIRECT ...` external
data, a variable name with a space, an unknown function or name, an INTEG rate
that is not a plain flow name or sum/difference of flow names, a subscript
equivalence `<->`) is reported in `import_problems` (code `E_SDIMPORT_UNSUPPORTED`) and
left out of the model rather than guessed at.

Returns {"ok", "model", "path", "import_problems": [{"code", "severity",
"message", "path", "hint"}], "errors", "warnings", "problems"} -- the last
three are the usual model-validation answer, over what DID translate.

name.description: Workspace name to load it under; defaults to the file stem.

path.description: Vensim (.mdl) file, relative to the workspace root.

name: import_mdl

description:
Write a model in the workspace to disk as JSON.

Call it once the model validates. A model created with `new_model` has no
path of its own, so the first save needs one.

Returns {"ok", "path", "errors", "warnings"}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to save.

path.description: Destination path under the workspace root; defaults to where it was opened.

name: save_model

description:
List the models currently open in the workspace, and the model files
available under the workspace root.

Use it to find out what you can `open_model` and which handles `get_model_summary`
and `run_model` accept.

Returns {"open": [{"name", "path", "blocks", "dirty", "has_results"}],
"files": [relative paths]}.
name: list_models

description:
A compact picture of a model: its blocks with their key parameters, its
links in branch order, its resources, and how many problems it has.

This is the tool to call before editing an existing model, and after a
batch of edits to check the shape is what you intended. It is deliberately
much smaller than `get_model_json`; reach for that only when you need every
field.

Returns {"model", "blocks", "links", "resources", "resource_sets",
"variables", "tables", "timeseries_inputs", "levels", "flows", "auxiliaries",
"delays", "schedules",
"failures", "scenarios", "simulation",
"errors", "warnings"}. Each link is "source -> target"; the ORDER of a block's
outgoing links is its branch order (branch 0 first).
name: get_model_summary

description:
The complete model layout as the JSON that would be saved to disk.

Use it only when `get_model_summary` is not enough -- a full layout is
large. It is also what you would hand to another tool that speaks the model
file format (see the `naga://reference/schema` resource).

Returns {"model", "layout"}.
name: get_model_json

description:
Add one block to a model and optionally set its parameters in the same
step (one undo entry).

The normal way to build a model: add CREATE, the processing blocks, and
DISPOSE, then `connect` them. Position is cosmetic -- call `auto_layout`
once at the end instead of placing blocks by hand.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"block": <the name it got>}. A wrong
param name or type comes back in "introduced" with code E_PARAM_UNKNOWN /
E_PARAM_TYPE and a hint listing the params this type takes.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Block name; auto-generated (create_1, process_2, ...) when omitted.

params.description: Parameter values to set on the block; the type's defaults fill the rest.

position.description: [x, y] canvas centre in scene units; auto-placed in a row when omitted.

name: add_block

description:
Change an existing block: merge parameters, rename it, move it, or
relabel it -- all as one undo entry.

`params` MERGES rather than replaces, so you can set one value without
restating the rest. Renaming rewires every link automatically.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"block": <name after the edit>}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Current name of the block to change.

new_name.description: Rename the block to this; every link follows the rename.

params.description: Parameters to merge into the block's existing params.

name: update_block

description:
Delete blocks and every link touching them, as one undo entry.

Unknown names are ignored rather than refused, so removing an already-gone
block is not an error. Expect new problems if you cut the flow in half --
the answer says which.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"removed": [names actually deleted]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

names.description: Block names to delete; their links go with them.

name: remove_blocks

description:
Link two blocks so entities flow from *source* to *target*, optionally
with a transfer delay.

Links are ORDERED: the n-th link you add out of a DECIDE is its branch n,
matching `probs[n]` / `conditions[n]`. Add branches in the order you want
them, or fix the order afterwards with `reorder_branches`. Only DECIDE and
LOGIC may have more than one outgoing link.

A branching block may send TWO branches to the same target (a DECIDE where
two cases end the same way): the second call returns `index` 1, which
`disconnect` takes to tell them apart.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"link": "source -> target", "index": n}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

source.description: Name of the block the entity leaves.

source_port.description: Out port name, only when the source is a SUBMODEL instance.

target.description: Name of the block the entity arrives at.

target_port.description: In port name, only when the target is a SUBMODEL instance.

name: connect

description:
Remove one link. A link that does not exist is a no-op, not an error.

Use it to rewire a flow -- for example to insert a new block between two
existing ones: disconnect a -> c, then connect a -> b and b -> c.

When several parallel links join the pair, name which one with *index*
(0 is the first); leaving it out is then an error listing the candidates.

Returns the usual edit answer.

index.description: Which of several parallel links between the pair, 0 first; only needed when there is more than one.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

source.description: Source block of the link to remove.

target.description: Target block of the link to remove.

name: disconnect

description:
Set the branch order of a block's outgoing links.

Branch order is what binds a DECIDE's `probs[n]` / `conditions[n]` to a
target, so getting it wrong sends entities down the wrong path without any
validation error. *order* must list exactly the current targets of *source*,
permuted.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"order": [...]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

order.description: Its target block names in the branch order you want, branch 0 first.

source.description: The branching block (a DECIDE or LOGIC).

name: reorder_branches

description:
REPLACE the model's whole resource table.

Use `upsert_record` (section "resources") for a single change; this one is
for setting several resources at once, or for deleting one by leaving it
out. A block's `resource_name` may name a resource or a resource set --
they share one namespace.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"resources": [names]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

resources.description: The complete resource list, each {"name", "capacity", "discipline", cost fields...}.

name: set_resources

description:
The JSON Schema of one record of *section*: what `upsert_record` expects.

The same `$defs/<item>` the model-file schema uses (MCP resource
naga://reference/schema), with the `$defs` it references. Read it once
before writing the first record of a section.

Returns {"section", "key", "def", "schema", "$defs"}.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: get_record_schema

description:
List every record of one section of the model, as stored.

Record sections: resources, resource_sets, schedules, failures, tables,
sequences, variables, entities, timeseries_inputs, levels, flows,
conversions, fixed_costs, fleets, motion_profiles, chargers, auxiliaries,
delays, subscripts, agent_types, populations, reality_checks and orders
(keyed by "id"; every other section by "name"). Record shape: schema
$defs/<item>, see get_record_schema.

Returns {"model", "section", "key", "records": [...]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: list_records

description:
Add a record to a section, or REPLACE the one with the same key.

The record is stored as given (record shape: schema $defs/<item>, see
get_record_schema) and the answer reports the validation problems the edit
introduced or fixed -- a missing field, a wrong type, a reference to
something undeclared. To change one field, list_records, edit, upsert.

Typical first records: a "resources" entry {"name", "capacity"} for a
PROCESS/SEIZE to seize; a "variables" entry {"name", "initial"} before an
expression reads it; a "tables" entry for TABLE("name", k); a "levels" and
a "flows" entry for continuous quantities. An agent type's `python` cannot
be written here: code needs the human's consent.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"section", "record": <key value>}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

record.description: The whole record, shaped as get_record_schema(section) says; its key field ("name", or "id" for orders) picks the record to replace.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: upsert_record

description:
Delete one record. References to it elsewhere (TABLE("name"), a flow's
"from", a block's resource_name, ...) come back as problems in the answer,
so fix them in the same batch.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"section", "removed": key}.

key.description: The record's key: its "name" (its "id" for orders).

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: remove_record

description:
Give the model REAL DATES, or remove them.

A calendar is optional: without one a model's clock is a plain number in the
base time unit, which is the right choice for an abstract study. Set one
when the study is about real weeks -- weekday shifts, a holiday shutdown, a
tariff or a campaign pinned to dates, or a client report that must say
"Wednesday 10:00". Once set, schedules may be authored as weekday grids,
time series and orders may carry ISO timestamps, and results, charts,
playback and exports all show wall-clock time.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"calendar": {...} or null}.

end.description: Optional ISO instant the run ends at, instead of a run-length number.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

start.description: ISO 8601 instant model time 0 stands for, e.g. "2026-01-05T06:00:00". With no offset it is read in `timezone`, never in local time. Pass null to remove the calendar.

timezone.description: IANA name such as UTC or Europe/Rome (default UTC). The wall clock weekday schedules and every date label use.

name: set_calendar

description:
Read a CSV under the workspace root into a lookup table.

Two shapes: a 1-D table is `key,value` under a `key,value` header; a 2-D
table is a header row of column keys whose first cell is EMPTY, then one
row per key. The file must be under the workspace root -- a path that
escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"table": name, "rows", "columns"}.

column_mode.description: Lookup mode for the column keys.

default.description: Value for a missing exact key.

key_mode.description: Lookup mode for the row keys: exact, step or linear.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Table name to create or replace.

path.description: CSV file under the workspace root.

name: upsert_table_from_csv

description:
List the model's time-series inputs, levels and flows in one answer.

A time series is a profile read by TS("name") -- a PV curve, a site load, a
tariff by hour. A level is a continuous quantity with bounds (battery
energy, tank volume, stock on hand), read by LEVEL("name"). A flow moves
quantity between levels at a rate that is an expression, read by
FLOW("name"). Call this before writing any of those expressions.

Auxiliaries (AUX("name")) and delays (DELAY("name")) are the system-dynamics
records that go with them.

Subscripts are the dimensions records run over. Edit any of these with
upsert_record / remove_record.

Returns {"model", "timeseries_inputs": [{"name", "points", "interpolation",
"beyond"}], "levels": [...], "flows": [...], "auxiliaries": [...],
"delays": [...], "subscripts": [...], "sd": {...} or null}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

name: list_continuous

description:
Read a `time,value` CSV under the workspace root into a time-series input.

The header row is optional. The file must be under the workspace root -- a
path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"series": name, "points": n}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Series name to create or replace.

path.description: CSV file under the workspace root, two columns: time and value.

time_unit.description: Unit the time column is in.

name: upsert_timeseries_input_from_csv

description:
The model's path network: the nodes assets sit on and the segments
vehicles and walkers drive along, with the shortest-path distance between
every pair of places.

Coordinates are layout coordinates -- metres once the model's background
image declares a scale. Travel time anywhere in the model is
`distance / speed` along this graph, so this is what to read before
reasoning about how long anything takes to move.

Returns {"model", "length_factor", "nodes": [...], "segments": [...],
"places": {name: node}, "unreachable": [[a, b], ...]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

name: get_network

description:
Add a network node, or move the one with this name.

A node is a PLACE: a dock door, an aisle junction, a pick face. Attach a
block to it with the STATION `node` param and travel to and from that
station becomes the shortest path along the segments.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"node": name}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Node name; a STATION's `node` param, a fleet's `home` and DISTANCE("...", ...) all address it by this.

x.description: Layout x coordinate (metres once the background declares a scale).

name: upsert_node

description:
Delete a network node AND the segments that used it (a segment with a
dangling end is not a thing a model can mean). Blocks whose `node` still
names it come back as E_NETWORK_NODE_UNKNOWN problems.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"removed": name}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Node to delete; every segment touching it goes with it.

name: remove_node

description:
Add a drivable segment between two nodes, or replace the one already
joining that ordered pair.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"segment": "source->target"}.

capacity.description: How many vehicles may be on it at once (zone control); omit for unlimited. Two-way with capacity 1 can deadlock head-on.

length.description: Length in layout units. Omit for the straight-line distance times the network's length_factor -- set it for a ramp, a curve or a detour.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

speed.description: Optional speed LIMIT on this segment. It changes travel TIME; the route chosen is still the shortest by length.

two_way.description: False makes it one-way from source to target.

name: upsert_segment

description:
Delete one segment. Check `get_network`'s "unreachable" afterwards: a
removal that strands a routing is an E_NETWORK_UNREACHABLE error.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"removed": "source->target"}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name: remove_segment

description:
Shortest path between two places on the model's network.

The same number `DISTANCE("source", "target")` returns in an expression, so
use it to sanity-check a travel time before writing one: a trip at speed v
takes `distance / v`.

Returns {"model", "from", "to", "distance", "path": [node, ...],
"reachable"}. `distance` is null when no path joins them.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

source.description: A node, a STATION block or a station alias.

target.description: Where the trip ends, named the same way.

name: get_distance

description:
List the model's routing sequences and the stations they visit.

A sequence is the operation order a product follows through shared
stations: a ROUTE block sends an entity whose `sequence`
attribute names one to each step's STATION block in turn. Call this
before writing a CREATE `sequence` or an ASSIGN to entity.sequence, so
the name and the stations are ones the model actually has.

Returns {"model", "sequences": [{"name", "steps": [{"station", "values"}]}],
"stations": [names of the model's STATION blocks]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

name: list_sequences

description:
List the model's orders: released jobs with a due date.

An order is "make `quantity` of `entity_type` on routing `sequence`,
released at `release`, due at `due`", both times in the model's BASE time
unit. A CREATE block in arrival mode "Orders" releases them; the run then
reports per-order lateness and tardiness and a model-wide service level.

Returns {"model", "orders": [...], "releases": [names of the CREATE blocks
in Orders mode]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

name: list_orders

description:
REPLACE (or extend) the model's orders from a CSV release list.

Columns: `id` (required), then any of release, due, quantity, entity_type,
sequence, priority, source; every other column becomes a free attribute
assigned onto the order's entities. This is the shape an MES work-order
export already has.

The file is read through the same root confinement as every other file
tool: a path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that
widens that.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"orders": <count>}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

path.description: CSV file to read, inside the workspace root.

replace.description: True (default) replaces the whole order book; False merges by id.

name: upsert_orders_from_csv

description:
REPLACE the model's entity-type table.

Entity types name the things flowing through the model (CREATE's `e_type`)
and carry the per-type WIP `holding_cost` used by the cost KPIs. A model
with no declared types still runs: everything is "DEFAULT".

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"entities": [names]}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name: set_entity_types

description:
Set the model's default run settings; only the arguments you pass change.

ALWAYS set a run length for a model that cannot drain on its own -- one with
an endless CREATE (max_arrivals 0), a failure, or a repeating capacity
schedule. Without it a run raises rather than hanging.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"simulation": {...}}.

currency.description: Cost label only; never enters the arithmetic.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

replications.description: How many independent replications a run does by default.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units; 0/null means "until the model drains". With a calendar you can set an end DATE instead, with set_calendar.

time_unit.description: The model's BASE unit: seconds, minutes, hours or days.

warmup.description: Time at which statistics are reset.

name: set_simulation_settings

description:
Turn on the system-dynamics step grid, change it, or remove it (dt null).

Without it a flow rate is re-evaluated only at events, which is exact for
rates that change only then. A rate that reads LEVEL(), FRACTION() or TNOW
-- dL/dt = -k*L, logistic growth, an SIR model -- needs the grid: it is
re-integrated every dt with Euler or RK4, the way Stella and Vensim do.
Static rates are untouched, and events inside a step stay exact.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"sd": {...} or null}.

dt.description: Step of the system-dynamics grid, > 0; null removes the grid.

method.description: euler (Stella/Vensim default) or rk4 (fourth order; no random draws in a dynamic rate).

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

time_unit.description: Unit dt is in: base (the model's own) or seconds/minutes/hours/days.

name: set_sd_settings

description:
Lay the model's blocks out left to right in a deterministic layered
arrangement, one undo entry.

Purely cosmetic -- it changes no behaviour and no KPI. Call it once after
building a model so a human opening it in the editor sees a readable
diagram instead of a pile of blocks.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"moved": <block count>}.
name: auto_layout

description:
Validate a model and return every problem with a stable code, a
JSON-pointer path, and a hint saying how to fix it.

Call this after each batch of edits and ALWAYS before running. Errors stop a
run; warnings (code prefix W_) do not, but usually point at a modelling
mistake. `requires_run_length` tells you whether the model can drain on its
own -- if it is true and the run length is 0, a run will be refused.

Returns {"model", "ok", "errors", "warnings", "requires_run_length",

loop at every step: a loop's relative score is its share of the change in
its stocks, signed (+ reinforcing, - balancing); the dominant loops at a
step are the fewest that explain at least half of it.

throughput-time series.

replication budget, then confirm the winner statistically.

Every factor is an override path plus a range, exactly like a scenario
override but varying. The budget is a HARD cap on replications, so start
small (a few hundred) and raise it if `converged` is false. Constraints are
judged on confidence intervals, so a point may come back "unknown" rather
than feasible or infeasible.

description:
Read the model's data bindings and report what each one produced.

A binding is "this parameter comes from that column of that file", so this
is how a model's numbers come from measurements instead of guesses. Nothing
here raises: a source that is missing, refused or unreadable comes back as
a `problem` on its own row and simply is not applied.

Files must be under the workspace root, and a `sql`/`json_url` source is
read only if the person who started this server allowed network access.
There is no argument that changes either: a refusal is final for you, and
its `problem` tells the HUMAN what to re-run if they want it.

Call with `apply=true` to write the values into the model (undoable), or
leave it false to preview. `run_model` does not resolve bindings by
default, but its own `bind_data=true` argument resolves `series:` and
`orders` bindings at RUN TIME -- those two never get written into
the model file even with `apply=true` here; see the E_DATA_BINDING_TARGET
hint below.

A `value` is what the binding read, and it is data from outside: it is cut
to 200 rows and 200 characters a text, and `value_cut` then says how much
was left out ({"rows", "characters"}; null when nothing was). `apply=true`
still writes the whole value.

"location", "column", "transform", "target", "value", "value_cut", "rows",
"source_time", "problem"}], "problems": n}.

Give the model a WARM START: work already in the system at t=0.

This is what makes a model a twin rather than a study. Entities are
injected into the named block in list order as if they had just arrived
there; `age` is how long an entity has already been in the system (its
reported time in system includes that history); `in_service: k` means the
first k are already being served, holding `remaining[i]` if you know the
residual service times -- give them when you do, since a fresh sample is
only exact for an exponential service.

A warm-started model needs no warm-up, and `run_model` defaults it to 0.
Pass no arguments to clear the initial state.

Tune model parameters until the model reproduces measured KPIs.

Give what the real system did (`targets`) and which parameters may move
(`factors`, the same shape `optimize` takes). The objective is the weighted
sum of squared RELATIVE errors, so KPIs on different scales count equally.
A target with a `tolerance` gets a pass/fail verdict; read the per-target
confidence interval too -- a pass whose interval is far wider than the
tolerance has not really been demonstrated.

Returns {"model", "best", "objective", "passed", "budget_used", "converged",
"overrides", "targets": [{"kpi", "observed", "simulated", "lb", "ub",

Forecast a short horizon from the model's CURRENT state, with
uncertainty bands and event probabilities.

Starts from the model's data bindings and initial state, runs a terminating
horizon with no warm-up, and answers "where is this heading". The band is
the empirical 5-95% range across replications -- where a single future run
is likely to land -- NOT a confidence interval of the mean, which is the
narrower `lb`/`ub` pair beside it.

An event's `kpi` may be any run KPI or a time-series peak,
`timeseries/<series>/max`, which is how you ask "was the queue EVER above
8" rather than "was it on average".

"ub", "q05", "q95", "min", "max"}], "events": [{"event", "kpi", "condition",

Write the last run's results to a file: an Excel workbook, CSV folder,

`json` when another program will read the numbers. Run the model first.

Evaluate a built-in controller against a Policy-mode DECIDE.

Runs `episodes` episodes of `nagasim.rl.SimEnv`, driving every pending
decision at the named `policy` with `controller`. Use this to compare
"shortest" against "random" (or "roundrobin") before ever training
anything, or to sanity-check a model's Policy-mode DECIDE wiring.

Returns {"model", "policy", "controller", "reward", "mean", "lb", "ub",
"episodes", "returns": [per-episode return] (capped)}.

Run a design of experiments and fit a response-surface surrogate over it
-- a fast stand-in for the simulation, for optimisation or
what-if exploration without spending more replications.

Every factor is swept per `design` and simulated `replications` times; the
surrogate is then fit on the point means, weighted by their precision.
Check `lack_of_fit` before trusting `suggest`-style extrapolation: it means
the model misses structure the replication noise does not explain, so
"quadratic" or "auto" (or "gp"/"forest" with scikit-learn) may do better
than "linear".

Returns {"model", "response", "kind", "n_points", "r2", "r2_adj",
"cv_rmse", "lack_of_fit", "coefficients": [{"term", "coefficient",
"std_error"}] (empty for gp/forest)}.

Undo the last edit to a model.

Every tool that changes a model pushes exactly one undo entry, so one
`undo` reverses one tool call. Use it to back out an edit whose returned
problems show it was wrong.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"can_undo", "can_redo", "label": the
undone edit's short name (e.g. "Add block"), or "Edit" for one with none}.

Redo the edit that `undo` reversed.

Only available while nothing new has been edited since the undo: any fresh
mutation clears the redo stack, exactly like the editor.

Returns the usual edit answer plus {"can_undo", "can_redo", "label": the
redone edit's short name}.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

name: redo

description:
Run one replication of a model under a debugger: start it, or continue it,
until a stop, one step, a model time, a pending decision or the end.

The run is kept between calls, one per model, so the usual loop is: set stops
and watches, call again and again, and read `debug_inspect` whenever it
returns. A stop fires on a change -- an entity entering a block, an expression
going from false to true -- so calling again always moves on. Nothing here
changes the results: a run that is stopped, stepped and inspected ends with the
same numbers as `run_model` with one replication and the same seed.

`back` undoes the previous call's move: the run is rebuilt where that call
found it, by replaying the same seed and decisions, so nothing is approximated.

`state` says why it returned: "back", "stop" (see `hits`), "step", "time" (reached
`to`), "decision" (a Policy DECIDE waits: answer with `decisions`; the clock
cannot move until you do), "budget" (max_seconds ran out; call again),
"horizon" or "drained" (the run is over; `restart` to debug again). `hits`
lists every stop that fired during the call and is read at every return, so
it can be non-empty beside any state, not only "stop".

A call is refused (E_BAD_ARGUMENT) before anything changes when `stops` or
`watches` is not a list, has more than 50 entries or holds a text of more than
500 characters, or `to` is not a finite number; a bad stop likewise
(E_BAD_STOP). Then a start or `restart` happens (with the new stops and watches,
if given), then `decisions` are applied, then on a continuing run the new stops
and watches take effect, then the run moves. A refused
decision answers with an error before the run moves: a continuing run keeps its
stops and watches as they were, but the decisions listed before the refused one
stay applied. A start or `restart` is not undone by a later error in the same
call.

Returns {"model", "t", "state", "hits": [{"stop": index, "block", "entity_id",
"entity_type"} (an entity stop's "block" is the block entered) or {"stop": index,
"expr"}] (the first 50) and "hits_total": how
many fired, "watches": {text: value or "error: ..."} for the watches and the
stop expressions, "pending": [{"id", "policy", "block", "t", "entity_id",
"options"}] (the first 50) and "pending_total": how many wait, "model_edited":
true when the model changed since this run began}.

back.description: True: go back to where the previous call left the run, exactly (it is replayed from the seed and the decisions made), and return without moving. The replay runs from t = 0 within max_seconds; when it does not fit, E_BUDGET and the run stays where it was. Not with `to`, `step`, `scope`, `decisions` or `restart`.

decisions.description: Answers to pending decisions: [{"policy", "option", "request_id"}] (request_id optional: the policy's oldest). Applied after the checks of the other arguments and after a start or `restart`, before the run moves.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget for this call; the run stays where it got to. 0 means no budget: the call runs until a stop, `to`, a decision or the end.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to debug.

restart.description: True: drop the run and start again from t = 0 on the model as it is now, keeping the stops and watches unless new ones are given.

scope.description: With `step`: a submodel instance (or a block); the step goes on to the next event of a block inside it, so it stays where you are looking.

seed.description: Seed of the run; read only when the run starts or restarts.

step.description: True: stop at the next event the trace shows (one entity move, one resource change).

stops.description: Replaces the stops (a list of at most 50, each text at most 500 characters): [{"block": name}] stops when an entity enters that block (a submodel instance name: anything inside it), [{"entity": id}] when that entity is created or moves, [{"expr": text}] when the expression becomes true. A block or entity stop may add "entity" (that entity only) and "when" (an expression read with the entering entity, e.g. 'entity.e_type == "Red"'). Omit to keep them, [] to clear.

to.description: Model time to run to at most (a finite number); omit for no time limit.

watches.description: Replaces the watch expressions, read at every return (a list of at most 50 texts of at most 500 characters). Omit to keep, [] to clear.

name: debug_run

description:
Read the state of a model's debug run where it stands, without moving it.

Call it after `debug_run` returns. With no argument it is the overview: how
many entities sit in each block, every resource's state, every level's value
and the decisions waiting. `block` adds that block's queue and entities;
`entity` adds one live entity's attributes, the model's own included.

Counts are per block of the top level: a block inside a submodel instance is
counted with its instance, and `block` then answers for the instance (see the
"name" it returns).

Returns {"model", "t", "pending" (the first 50), "pending_total", "counts":
{block: entities}, "resources": {name: {"state", "busy", "capacity"}},
"levels": {name: value}, "model_edited": true when the model changed since the
run began, in which case the run still answers for the model it was built
from}; with `block`: "block": {"name", "count", "in_service", "queue": [entity
ids waiting, oldest first], "entities": [ids]} (50 ids at most each); with
`entity`: "entity": {"id", "type", "created", "attributes"}, or null once it
is disposed or inside a batch.

block.description: A block or submodel instance to look into; omit for the overview only.

entity.description: Id of an entity to read (from a hit, a queue or `pending`).

model.description: Workspace name of a model with a debug run.

name: debug_inspect

description:
Check a plant mapping against a model and, given a recorded plant log,
say what the plant looked like at the log's last instant.

A plant mapping says what each key a plant sends asserts about the model
(which block an item is in, how many units of a resource are busy, what a
level holds). The log's observations become the same trace events a run
emits, so `blocks` and `resources` read exactly like a run's playback.

Both files are data under the workspace root. This tool opens no
connection and has no argument that could: watching a live plant is the
person's own `naga plant watch` with their connections file.

`counts` says what was dropped, repaired or made up, by reason; `problems`
carries the mapping's errors (then nothing is replayed) and the replay's
warnings.

Returns {"model", "signals", "problems"} and, with a log, {"observations",
"events", "truncated", "now", "stamp", "entities", "counts", "blocks":
{block: items}, "resources": [{"name", "state", "busy", "capacity"}]}.

log.description: Recorded plant log (one JSON object a line, as `naga watch --record` writes), a path relative to the workspace root. Empty: only check the mapping.

mapping.description: Plant mapping (*.plantmap.json), a path relative to the workspace root.

model.description: Workspace name of the model the mapping is for.

name: get_plant_timeline

description:
What the plant looks like now, as the running twin last wrote it.

A twin is started by a person (`naga twin run`), reads their plant through
their connections and writes a result every few seconds; this tool reads
that result and nothing else. `sources` says whether each source is live
and how old its last word is; `view` holds the items in each block, each
resource's state and the levels at model time `at` (`approximate` is true
when the plant names no items, so counts are estimates; `counters` is what
the plant itself counted as having left a block since the twin first saw
that counter, observed and not estimated); `problems` are
coded, with what the twin did about each. Check `written` before trusting
the picture: a twin that stopped leaves its last result behind, and one
that runs writes every `cadence.every` seconds (null: it is run one step
at a time by a scheduler). `at` is model time, in `model.time_unit` from
`model.epoch` (null where the source has no epoch).

Returns {"cycle", "written", "started", "cadence": {"every",
"forecast_every"}, "model": {"name", "hash", "time_unit", "epoch"}, "at", "stamp",
"sources": [{"name", "state", "age", "lost", "gaps"}], "view": {"approximate",
"wip", "blocks", "in_service", "resources", "levels", "counters"}, "mapped", "problems":
[{"code", "severity", "message", "path", "hint"}]}.
name: get_twin_monitor

description:
The running twin's latest forecast, and how its earlier ones compare
with what the plant then did.

`forecast.status` is "ok", "running", "skipped" (a source is down),
"refused" (the model cannot be started from the plant's state: `reason`
and the monitor's problems say which kind), "failed" or "none"; with any
status but "ok" the record shown is the last good one. The record names
what it was computed from (`state` and `model` hashes, `seed`, `from`,
`horizon`, `replications`), so it can be reproduced; `finished` and `took`
(seconds) say when it could first be read and how long it ran. `kpis` are
end-of-horizon means with a confidence interval (`lb`, `ub`) and the 5-95%
band of single replications; `points` are predictions at stated times.
`comparison` sets each prediction whose time has come beside the observed
value: `inside` says whether it fell in the 5-95% band. `approximate` is
about counts of items inferred where the plant names none (`system/WIP`
then rests on estimates); a `block/<name>/out` row is what the plant's own
counter counted and is observed either way. `scores` sums those
comparisons by series and lead (how far ahead, in model time): `coverage`
is the share inside the band (`nominal`, 0.9, when the model is right; a
row with `whole` true holds whole numbers only and covers more than that
on a right model, so compare its `pinball`), `bias` the mean of observed
minus forecast mean, `error` the mean absolute error, `pinball` the
quantile loss of the band (lower is better). Never quote a row without
`basis` (forecasts, points, `missed` because the twin was late or a source
not ready, `lost` because a counter lost count, since when; `same_seed`
forecasts are not independent samples), and say `reason` when there are no
rows. Readings overlap in time: this is evidence in distribution, not a
test. When `forecast.actions` is there, the forecast ASSUMES actions a
person took through the twin's outbox are in the plant (`assumes` says so
in words; `get_twin_recommendations` lists them under `standing`): say so
whenever you quote such a forecast.

Returns {"cycle", "written", "model", "forecast": {"status", "reason",
"state", "model", "seed", "from", "stamp", "horizon", "replications",
"approximate", "finished", "took", "kpis": [...], "points": [...]},
"comparison": [{"state",
"series", "at", "mean", "q05", "q95", "observed", "observed_at", "inside"}],
"scores": {"nominal", "basis": {"forecasts", "same_seed", "points", "missed",
"lost", "since", "first", "last"}, "reason", "rows": [{"series", "lead",
"points", "missed", "lost", "whole", "coverage", "bias", "error",
"pinball"}]}}.
name: get_twin_forecast

description:
What the running twin recommends now, and what became of what it
recommended before. Read-only: this tool cannot deliver, approve, reject
or address a recommendation, and no tool can.

The person who started the twin gave it candidate actions and one KPI
(`kpi`, with `better`: "higher" or "lower"). After each forecast the twin
runs every candidate from the same plant state on the same random numbers
(`crn`) and sets it beside doing nothing. An item has its `action`
({"verb", "target", "value"}), `baseline` and `with_action` (means of the
KPI), `effect` (the mean difference) with its 95% interval (`low`, `high`),
`confidence` (the share of replications in which the action did better)
and a `verdict`: "better" (the interval excludes no effect), "no_effect"
(it includes it: do not present this as a gain), "worse", "failed" or
"standing" (already taken). Only "better" items have a `rank`, an `id` and
a `status`: "proposed" (shown, not delivered), "delivered" (written to the
person's own outbox, unanswered), "taken", "rejected", "expired" or
"dropped". With `status` "none", say `reason`: "no_forecast" (a source is
down or the state was refused: see `get_twin_forecast`), "none_better",
"kpi", "replications" or "failed". `standing` lists the actions a person
took, which every later forecast now assumes until a person ends one
(`ended` lists those). `effects` is what the plant's
own counter then showed over one horizon (`observed`), and whether that fell
in the 5-95% band the twin gave (`inside_interval`); "missed", "lost" and
"not_observable" say why there is no number. This is what the model says,
in distribution: not a causal claim about the plant, and one effect outside
its band proves little. A proposal is acted on by a person, in their own
queue or in the editor; if asked to approve or send one, say that you
cannot.

Returns {"cycle", "written", "model", "recommend": {"kpi", "better",
"level", "crn", "measurable", "status", "reason", "state", "seed",
"replications", "from", "stamp", "took", "reproducible", "items": [...],
"standing": [{"id", "action", "since"}], "ended": [{"id", "action",
"since", "ended"}], "effects": [{"id", "action",
"status", "observed", "inside_interval", "from", "until", "q05", "q95"}],
"outbox": {"sink", "state", "why", "records", "replies"}}}; `recommend` is
null for a twin that was given no candidates.

description:
Test one model step: write the whole model, run it, check it, and store it as a new
version (or as a draft when it fails). Always send the complete model file and a one-line
note. A model that does not validate or run is stored as a draft with its problems, not
refused: read "problems", fix the model, step again.

The replications come from a precision target, not from the model's own
simulation.replications: a first pass of 10, then, if a goal KPI's 95% confidence interval is
wider than its target, one rerun (same seed) with the count the widest needs, up to the size's
cap (quick 50, standard 200, deep 1000). The target is a relative half-width (quick 10%,
standard 5%, deep 2%; set another with study_update precision={"relative": 0.03}) or an
absolute one per goal ("precision": 0.5 in the KPI's unit). With no goal KPI the count is 10
and provisional. A cap reached makes the "precision" check partial, never failed.

The model's "scenarios" (a list of {"name", "overrides": [{"path":
"resources.<name>.capacity", "value": 2}]}) run with the step, with the same replications
and seed, up to the size's cap; their goal KPIs and goals met come back in "scenarios".

`changes` (the same keys and shapes as study_update) is recorded first, in the same call, so
a step that also records the goals or a validation needs one call, not two. Scenario
overrides sent as {"resources.<name>.capacity": 2} are mapped to the list shape; a target
component without blocks whose name matches a block name is mapped to it. Both are listed in
"normalised". Example: study_step(study="naga-studies/cranes", layout={...the whole model...},
note="add the second crane", changes={"assumptions": [{"id": "a1", "text": "...", "source": "..."}]}).

A tail goal {"id", "text", "kpi": "<resource>/Time in Queue", "share_above": 15, "high": 0.05}
bounds the share of entities that waited more than 15 at that resource. The engine rebuilds
the waits from the run's resource log (FIFO resources only) and stores the share per
replication as the KPI "<resource>/Share waiting over 15", with its confidence interval, so it is
judged, sized (precision) and compared across scenarios like any KPI. When the waits cannot be
rebuilt the goal stays not_verified and "tail_note" says why.

Returns {"id", "kind": "version"|"draft", "verdict", "checks", "changes", "kpis",
"replications", "precision": {goal KPI: {half_width, target, met}}, "precision_note" (one
sentence), "sufficiency", "next_step"}. A version has no
report file by default (the answer is the light output); study_report writes it on request. With scenarios: "scenarios": {name: {"kpis": {goal KPI: {mean,
ci_half_width}}, "goals": {goal id: met|not_met|not_verified}}}, and "scenario_error" or
"scenarios_skipped" when a run failed or the cap cut some; "normalised" when an input was mapped.

run length (warm-up 10% of that, 10 replications, seed 0), compares the mean wait in queue
with M/M/c (Erlang C) or M/G/1 (Pollaczek-Khinchine) and records a known_answer validation
that passes within 5% relative error. Any other model answers E_STUDY_NOT_APPLICABLE with the
reason, so the person is asked for another validation.
